claims.text: The initial HEA is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with uniformly distributed elements.
High mechanical loading induces local elemental segregation or nanoscale precipitation in the initially single-phase HEA.
Trace interstitial impurities can trigger or exacerbate nanoscale precipitation or phase segregation.
The segregation or precipitation is localized at dislocation walls and grain boundaries.
The localized precipitates or separated phases act as stress concentrators.
The localized precipitates or separated phases impede dislocation mobility.
Phase segregation and depletion of solute from the matrix reduce the effectiveness of initial solid-solution strengthening.
Local compositional inhomogeneity creates brittle zones in which microcracks nucleate and propagate.
The proposed microstructural changes cause an overall loss of toughness and a transition toward brittle fracture.
The undeformed or minimally stressed baseline HEA has high ductility and toughness.
The baseline condition exhibits ductile dimpled fracture morphology.
Mechanically loaded specimens will develop detectable nanoscale compositional or phase inhomogeneity relative to the baseline.
Mechanically loaded specimens will have reduced strain hardening relative to the baseline.
Mechanically loaded specimens will have reduced fracture toughness and ductility relative to the baseline.
Mechanically loaded specimens will exhibit cleavage or quasi-cleavage fracture features rather than predominantly dimpled fracture.
The proposed behavior applies under high cyclic or static loading when substantial strain accumulates.
The mechanism may not apply below the stress or deformation range required to trigger measurable segregation.
A same-alloy comparison between highly loaded and unloaded specimens, optionally stratified by impurity level, is the proposed controlled test.
The mechanism is falsified if loaded specimens show neither statistically significant segregation or precipitation nor deterioration in toughness or ductility relative to the baseline.
